title: The Strength of Weak Ties
text:
In the late 1960s, the sociologist Mark Granovetter, then a graduate student at Harvard, interviewed and surveyed professional, technical and managerial workers in Newton, a suburb of Boston, who had recently changed jobs. He wanted to know how they had found their new positions.

Many had heard about the job through a personal contact. But when Granovetter asked how often they had seen that contact around the time of the job change, the answer was surprising. Only a minority, about one in six, had seen the person often. Most had seen them only occasionally, and more than a quarter rarely. The decisive tip had come not from close friends, but from old college classmates, former colleagues and people they barely knew.

In his 1973 paper, Granovetter explained why. Close friends tend to know each other and move in the same circles, so they mostly hear the same news you already know. Acquaintances are bridges to other circles, carrying information that would otherwise never reach you. A network rich in weak ties, he argued, connects people to the wider world, while one made only of strong ties can leave a person or a community isolated.
lesson: Acquaintances are not second-class relationships. Keep in touch with former colleagues and people you meet occasionally, because they connect you to opportunities your close friends never hear about.
source: Granovetter, M. S. (1973). The strength of weak ties. American Journal of Sociology, 78(6), 1360-1380.
